title: SSD, NVMe & Storage Hardware
summary: Modern storage hardware—SSDs, NVMe drives, and emerging persistent memory—has fundamentally different performance characteristics from the spinning disks that shaped classical database and OS design. NVMe SSDs deliver sub-100μs random read latency and millions of IOPS, but exhibit asymmetric read/write performance, write amplification, and garbage collection pauses that production systems must account for. Understanding NAND flash internals, the NVMe protocol, I/O scheduling, and emerging tiered storage architectures allows engineers to match workloads to storage appropriately and avoid the trap of treating SSDs as fast HDDs.

sections.title: NAND Flash Internals: Why SSDs Behave Differently from HDDs
paragraphs: NAND flash stores data as charge in floating-gate transistors. Bits are read by measuring the charge level—SLC (Single-Level Cell) stores 1 bit (two levels), MLC stores 2 bits (four levels), TLC stores 3 bits (eight levels), QLC stores 4 bits (sixteen levels). More bits per cell means lower cost per GB but worse performance, endurance, and reliability. Consumer SSDs use TLC or QLC; enterprise SSDs use MLC or TLC with higher over-provisioning. Cloud instance store SSDs are enterprise-grade NVMe devices, typically MLC or high-endurance TLC.

The asymmetry between reading and writing is NAND flash's fundamental property. Reading is fast (50–100 μs for page read). Writing is fast to SLC cache but slow (1–3 ms) for direct program operations on TLC/QLC cells—the NAND must first erase the entire block (512 KB to 4 MB) before writing any page within it. Writes happen at page granularity (4–16 KB); erases happen at block granularity. This erase-before-write constraint means the SSD's Flash Translation Layer (FTL) must do log-structured writes: new data is always written to clean (erased) blocks; old blocks are recycled asynchronously via garbage collection.

Write amplification (WA) is the ratio of physical bytes written to the SSD vs logical bytes written by the host. If you write 4 KB of data, the FTL might need to read-modify-write an entire 128 KB block (reading 124 KB of valid data, writing 128 KB to a new block). WA = 128/4 = 32. High write amplification reduces SSD endurance (each cell has a finite write cycle count: MLC ~3000, TLC ~1000, QLC ~500) and reduces sustained write throughput. Workloads with small random writes (databases, logging, event processing) have high WA; sequential write workloads have WA near 1.

Over-provisioning is spare capacity reserved by the SSD (not visible to the OS) to absorb write amplification and maintain garbage collection parallelism. Consumer SSDs: ~7% OP. Enterprise SSDs: 28% OP. Higher OP means lower steady-state WA, more consistent performance under sustained writes, and longer endurance. For NVMe SSDs used as database transaction logs, consider enterprise drives with 28%+ OP or manually over-provision by leaving 20–30% of the drive unpartitioned.
bullets: NAND endurance: MLC ~3000 P/E cycles; TLC ~1000; QLC ~500; enterprise TLC with OP: ~3000+
Block size: 128 KB–4 MB (varies by NAND); must erase before write; erase is the bottleneck for sustained writes
Over-provisioning: leave 20–30% unpartitioned on consumer SSDs used for write-intensive workloads

sections.title: NVMe Protocol and Performance Characteristics
paragraphs: NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) is a protocol designed for NAND flash, replacing SATA/SAS which were designed for HDDs. SATA supports 1 command queue with 32 slots; NVMe supports 65,535 queues with 65,535 slots each. This parallelism directly maps to NAND flash's internal parallelism—modern SSDs have 8–32 NAND packages, each with multiple dies, chips, and planes. NVMe allows the CPU to submit and receive I/O completions without locking (using memory-mapped registers and PCIe DMA), reducing per-I/O overhead from ~8 μs (SATA) to ~2 μs (NVMe).

NVMe Gen 4 (PCIe 4.0) SSDs achieve: ~7 GB/s sequential read, ~5 GB/s sequential write, ~1 million IOPS random read, ~700k IOPS random write, ~100 μs 4K random read latency. NVMe Gen 5 (PCIe 5.0, 2023): ~14 GB/s sequential, ~1.5M IOPS. For comparison, SATA SSD: ~550 MB/s sequential, ~100k IOPS, ~100 μs. HDD: ~150 MB/s sequential, ~200 IOPS random, ~8 ms. The gap in random IOPS—NVMe vs HDD—is 5,000×. Database index lookups that would take seconds on HDD take milliseconds on NVMe.

Latency variance (tail latency) on SSDs is significant. Garbage collection pauses cause p99 latency spikes: 4K random reads might be 100 μs at p50 but 1–10 ms at p99 during GC. Enterprise SSDs with dedicated GC management (Intel P5800X, Samsung PM9A3) have more consistent p99 latency. Cloud provider SSDs (AWS EBS io2 Block Express, GCP pd-extreme) advertise 99.9th percentile latency SLAs of 1–2 ms for 4K random reads. For applications sensitive to tail latency (trading systems, real-time analytics), drive selection based on p99 matters as much as peak IOPS.

NVMe namespaces partition the physical SSD into logical devices for multi-tenant environments. A single NVMe drive can expose multiple namespaces, each with its own namespace ID and capacity. Cloud providers use this to slice a single NVMe device among multiple VMs or containers. Namespaces can share or isolate resources; NVMe 1.4's I/O determinism feature allows QoS policies per namespace, guaranteeing minimum IOPS to each tenant.
bullets: NVMe queue depth: 65k queues × 65k entries; vs SATA: 1 queue × 32 entries
NVMe Gen 4 peak: 7 GB/s sequential, 1M IOPS, ~100μs 4K random read
GC pause p99: 1–10ms on consumer SSDs; enterprise SSDs with dedicated GC achieve <1ms p99

sections.title: Linux I/O Scheduler and NVMe Optimization
paragraphs: Linux I/O schedulers are designed around different storage characteristics. The 'none' scheduler submits I/O directly to the block device in submission order—optimal for NVMe drives, which have their own internal queue management and don't benefit from OS-level reordering. The 'mq-deadline' scheduler enforces fairness by promoting old I/O requests that would otherwise starve; useful for HDD or SATA SSD with limited queue depth. The 'kyber' scheduler targets latency for heterogeneous mixed read/write workloads. Check and configure with: cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler.

io_depth (queue depth) must match the device's capability. For NVMe, optimal io_depth is typically 32–128 for throughput-maximized workloads; each queued I/O is dispatched to a different NAND die in parallel. For latency-sensitive applications (trading, online transactions), lower io_depth (1–4) reduces queuing delay. The PostgreSQL max_io_concurrency parameter controls I/O parallelism per query; set it to match the NVMe's internal parallelism (32–64) for analytical workloads, 1 for OLTP.

Direct I/O (O_DIRECT) bypasses the Linux page cache and reads/writes directly between application buffers and the NVMe device. Databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, RocksDB) use O_DIRECT to manage their own buffer pool without double-buffering: data is not cached in both the OS page cache and the database buffer pool. Without O_DIRECT, a 32 GB database with a 32 GB buffer pool might consume 64 GB of memory. Direct I/O requires 512-byte-aligned buffers (or 4096-byte-aligned for 4Kn drives); misaligned I/O fails with EINVAL.

Filesystem choice affects NVMe performance. ext4 is safe and well-tested but its journal adds write amplification (data journaling mode: 2× writes for small transactions; ordered mode: 1× for data, journal for metadata). XFS has better scalability for concurrent I/O and large files. For latency-critical workloads, f2fs (Flash-Friendly File System) is designed around NAND's erase-before-write semantics, performing better for mixed small-file workloads. For databases, raw block devices or loop-mounted files with O_DIRECT bypass the filesystem entirely.
bullets: I/O scheduler for NVMe: 'none' is optimal; 'mq-deadline' for mixed HDD/SSD
O_DIRECT: bypasses page cache; requires 512/4096-byte aligned buffers; used by all production databases
ext4 data journaling mode: 2× writes (journal + data); switch to 'ordered' for write-heavy NVMe workloads

sections.title: Cloud Storage: EBS, Instance Store, and Object Storage
paragraphs: Cloud block storage (AWS EBS, GCP Persistent Disk, Azure Managed Disks) separates storage from compute. EBS volumes are network-attached—I/O crosses the VPC network to a storage server. This adds ~100–200 μs of network latency on top of the SSD's own ~100 μs, making EBS 2–3× higher latency than local NVMe. EBS throughput is also network-limited: an io2 Block Express volume provides max 256k IOPS, while a local NVMe SSD provides 1M+ IOPS. The benefit: EBS volumes survive instance termination, can be resized, snapshotted, and mounted on other instances.

Instance store provides physically attached NVMe SSDs (on i3, i4, r5d, z1d, and other instance types). Instance store latency is ~100–200 μs (NVMe), and throughput can reach 7+ GB/s on large instances. The critical limitation: instance store data is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated. Instance store is appropriate for: temporary compute storage (sort spill files, intermediate join results), write-intensive ephemeral data (short-lived indexes, staging areas for ETL), and distributed systems that replicate data across instances (Cassandra, HDFS, Kafka).

Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) is the cheapest and most scalable tier but with fundamentally different access patterns: HTTP-based, eventually consistent (for some operations), and optimized for large objects. S3 GET latency is 10–100 ms for the first byte (time-to-first-byte), compared to microseconds for block storage. S3 Express One Zone improves this to 2–4 ms. Object storage is not appropriate for random small I/O patterns (database page reads) but excellent for: analytical data lakes (Parquet, ORC files read by Spark/Athena), model checkpoints, backup targets, and infrequently accessed archives. The tiered storage pattern—hot data on NVMe, warm on EBS, cold on S3—is ubiquitous in cloud data architecture.
bullets: EBS latency: network-attached; 200–400μs end-to-end; local NVMe: 100μs
Instance store: ~100–200μs latency, 7+ GB/s throughput; data lost on instance stop/terminate
S3 TTFB: 10–100ms; S3 Express One Zone: 2–4ms; not suitable for random 4K database I/O

sections.title: Storage Tiering and Modern Patterns
paragraphs: Tiered storage automatically moves data between storage tiers based on access frequency. Hot-to-warm-to-cold tiering is used by object stores (S3 Intelligent-Tiering), databases (MySQL InnoDB's tiered buffer pool), and ML platforms (DL model caching). The tiering decision is based on last-access time and access frequency; data accessed less than once in 30 days moves to Infrequent Access; not accessed for 90 days moves to Glacier/Archive. Rehydration from Glacier adds 1–12 hours of latency—plan for this in recovery SLAs.

Local NVMe + remote object storage is the dominant cloud database pattern. ClickHouse, Redshift, BigQuery, and Snowflake separate compute (NVMe SSDs for caching) from storage (S3/GCS for durability). The database reads data from S3 into local NVMe cache on first query; subsequent queries are served from cache. Cache hit rates of 90–95% make this competitive with local storage for many analytical workloads. The benefit: unlimited storage scalability via S3 at $0.023/GB vs NVMe at $0.20–0.80/GB.

NVMe over Fabrics (NVMeoF) extends the NVMe protocol over TCP/RDMA networks, allowing NVMe drives to be accessed remotely with near-local latency. NVMeoF/TCP adds 50–100 μs over a 25 GbE network vs ~100 μs for local NVMe—2× higher latency but unlimited distance. This is used in disaggregated storage architectures where storage nodes and compute nodes are separate, sharing NVMe capacity across the cluster. AWS EBS io2 Block Express is internally implemented on NVMeoF.
bullets: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: auto-moves objects between Standard (11 9s, $0.023/GB) and IA ($0.0125/GB) based on access
ClickHouse local disk cache: NVMe cache for remote S3 data; 10–50× read speedup for cached data
NVMeoF/TCP latency: ~200μs over 25GbE vs ~100μs local NVMe; viable for disaggregated storage

core.title: NAND Flash and Write Amplification
paragraphs: NAND flash requires erase-before-write at block granularity (128 KB–4 MB). The FTL does log-structured writes to avoid in-place updates. Write amplification (WA) = physical bytes written / logical bytes written; can reach 10–50× for small random writes.
TLC/QLC cells are cheaper but have lower endurance (1000/500 P/E cycles) and higher WA vs MLC. Over-provisioning reduces WA and GC pressure; enterprise drives have 28% OP vs consumer 7%.
GC pauses cause p99 latency spikes (1–10ms on consumer SSDs). Enterprise drives with dedicated GC management maintain sub-1ms p99.
bullets: P/E cycle: one program-erase cycle; MLC ~3000; TLC ~1000; QLC ~500
WA for 4K random writes: 10–50× on consumer TLC SSD; 2–5× on enterprise with high OP
TRIM command: tells SSD which blocks are free after file deletion; enables proactive GC

core.title: NVMe Performance and Linux I/O
paragraphs: NVMe provides 65k queues × 65k slots, mapping to NAND's internal parallelism. Gen 4 NVMe achieves 7 GB/s sequential, 1M IOPS, 100μs 4K random read latency.
Linux I/O scheduler: 'none' is optimal for NVMe; O_DIRECT bypasses page cache; databases require aligned buffers.
io_depth 32–128 maximizes NVMe throughput by keeping internal queues full; io_depth 1–4 minimizes queuing latency for OLTP.
bullets: fio benchmark: measure NVMe baseline with --direct=1 --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=32
O_DIRECT requirement: 512-byte or 4096-byte buffer alignment depending on drive logical block size
NVMe namespace: logical partition of physical SSD; supports QoS per namespace

core.title: Cloud Storage Tiers
paragraphs: EBS: network-attached, 200–400μs latency; survives instance stop; snapshots available. Instance store: local NVMe, 100–200μs, lost on stop/terminate.
S3: 10–100ms TTFB; $0.023/GB; appropriate for large objects, analytics, model storage. Not suitable for random 4K I/O.
Tiered storage pattern: hot data on local NVMe cache, warm on EBS, cold on S3. Used by ClickHouse, Snowflake, Redshift.
bullets: EBS gp3 baseline: 3000 IOPS; io2 Block Express: up to 256k IOPS
S3 multipart upload: required for objects >5 GB; optimal part size 100MB–1GB
S3 Transfer Acceleration: CloudFront edge uploads for globally distributed sources

deepDive.title: FTL Internals and Production SSD Behavior
paragraphs: The Flash Translation Layer (FTL) is the SSD's internal controller firmware that maps logical block addresses (LBAs) to physical NAND addresses. The FTL maintains a mapping table in DRAM (8–32 GB on enterprise drives for a 32 TB drive). If the mapping table is too large to fit in DRAM, the FTL uses a hierarchical mapping scheme (page-level for hot data, block-level for cold data). A large SSD starting from an empty state performs very differently than the same SSD in a 'steady state' (fully written once, GC ongoing)—benchmarks that only test 'fresh out of box' behavior are misleading for production planning.

Secure erase and sanitize commands (NVMe Format NVM, Sanitize) cryptographically erase all data on the drive. For cloud environments, all storage volumes must be sanitized before reuse. Cloud providers sanitize drives between customer tenants; instance store volumes are sanitized on termination. Secure erase is also the fastest way to restore 'fresh' SSD performance after heavy write workloads—a fully over-written SSD with no GC debt starts fresh. This is used by some database operators who reprovision SSDs quarterly to maintain write performance.

SLC cache on TLC/QLC SSDs: manufacturers reserve a portion of NAND cells to operate in SLC mode (single-level, highest performance). Writes go to SLC cache first (~1 GB/s, low latency), then are flushed to TLC/QLC in background. When SLC cache is exhausted (small cache on budget drives, large cache on premium drives), write performance drops to TLC/QLC program speed (~500 MB/s, higher latency). For sustained write workloads exceeding the SLC cache size, benchmark SLC-exhausted throughput, not burst.
bullets: FTL mapping table: ~1 GB DRAM per 1 TB of NAND at 4-byte entry per 4KB page
Steady-state benchmark: pre-condition SSD with 2× capacity sequential writes before benchmarking
SLC cache: ~100GB on consumer drives; ~200GB+ on enterprise; monitor with S.M.A.R.T. attribute 'media wearout indicator'

deepDive.title: Storage Optimization for Databases
paragraphs: RocksDB's key-value compaction generates heavy write amplification. LSM-tree compaction reads L0 data, merges with L1, and writes the result—potentially writing 10–30× the original data size. On a 2 TB NVMe SSD with 1000 P/E cycles, continuous 10× WA writing at 100 MB/s compaction = 1 TB/s raw write rate × 86400 s/day = 86 PB/day written. At 2 TB × 1000 P/E = 2 PB total write capacity, the drive would last ~8 hours. Real-world RocksDB WA is 10–30×, not theoretical maximum, but SSD wear is a real production concern for write-heavy LSM workloads—enterprise SSDs with high endurance are required.

PostgreSQL's storage engine was designed for HDDs. Random 8K page reads are the common case for index lookups; random writes are common for heap updates. For NVMe SSDs, the HDD-era optimization of sequential I/O over random I/O is unnecessary—NVMe random I/O is as fast as sequential. This means PostgreSQL's VACUUM (which rewrites heap pages sequentially) doesn't need to be as aggressive as on HDD systems; turning down autovacuum frequency reduces write amplification without the performance cliff that would occur on HDD.

WAL (Write-Ahead Log) placement: separating WAL from data on different NVMe devices doubles the available write throughput. WAL writes are sequential and latency-sensitive; data writes are random and throughput-sensitive. On a single NVMe device, WAL and data writes compete for the same queue. On separate devices, they're fully parallel. For PostgreSQL, Cassandra commitlog, and MySQL binlog, placing WAL on a dedicated NVMe device improves transaction throughput by 20–50%.
bullets: RocksDB write amplification: 10–30× typical; monitor with ROCKSDB_WRITE_AMP internal stat
NVMe SSD endurance monitoring: use nvme-cli smart-log to check data_units_written and percentage_used
WAL on dedicated NVMe: separate sequential WAL I/O from random data I/O for higher transaction throughput

expert.title: Zoned Storage and Emerging NVMe Features
paragraphs: ZNS (Zoned Namespace) NVMe SSDs expose the NAND's zone structure directly to the host, eliminating the FTL's internal mapping and GC. Each zone is a contiguous region that must be written sequentially and reset before reuse—the FTL is essentially moved to the application. Databases like RocksDB, in collaboration with WD and Seagate, have been adapted to use ZNS—RocksDB's LSM-tree compaction naturally writes sequentially, mapping well to ZNS zones. Benefits: 2–5× lower WA, more predictable latency (no GC pauses), 20–40% higher throughput for sequential write workloads. ZNS drives are production-grade as of 2022.

Computational storage devices (CSD) embed processing capabilities in the NVMe drive itself—simple RISC-V or ARM processors running on the drive can execute filter operations, decompression, and sorting on data before returning it to the host CPU. This reduces PCIe bandwidth consumption and host CPU overhead for data-intensive scan operations. Samsung's SmartSSD and Western Digital's OpenFlex are early products. For analytical queries that touch terabytes of cold data on inexpensive QLC SSDs, computational storage can filter 90% of data before it crosses the PCIe bus—a 10× bandwidth reduction.

Persistent Memory (PMem) in production: post-Intel Optane discontinuation (2022), persistent memory remains in the market via products from Micron and emerging CXL-attached DRAM. The key characteristic—byte-addressable persistence—enables a new class of storage architecture: data structures live in persistent memory, eliminating serialization, deserialization, and buffer management entirely. VoltDB, SAP HANA, and Redis Enterprise have PMem-aware modes that map their data structures directly into PMem address space. The challenge: PMem programming requires explicit cache line flushing (clflush, clflushopt) and memory barriers (sfence) for durability; standard writes may stay in CPU cache without reaching PMem.

examples.title: RocksDB on NVMe: Compaction Write Amplification
examples.description: A production RocksDB deployment at a fintech company was replacing NVMe SSDs every 6 months due to wear. Using nvme-cli smart-log, the data_units_written counter showed 20 PB written to a 2 TB drive (10× nominal capacity). Investigation revealed L0→L1 compaction WA of 25×. Mitigations: increasing L0 file count threshold (reduces compaction frequency), enabling compression (reduces data size), and using enterprise NVMe with 3× higher P/E cycle rating. After tuning, drive lifetime extended to 24 months.

examples.title: PostgreSQL on EBS vs Instance Store
examples.description: An e-commerce database on EBS io2 achieved 50k IOPS at 300μs average latency. For a Black Friday sale, the team moved to an i4i.8xlarge with local NVMe instance store (3.75 TB, 850k IOPS). Read latency dropped to 95μs and write commit latency dropped 70%. The tradeoff: full streaming replication to a Postgres replica on EBS ensured durability. The primary ran on fast ephemeral storage; failover was to the EBS replica. Transaction throughput increased 2× at p99.

examples.title: ClickHouse with S3 Object Storage + NVMe Cache
examples.description: A data platform team replaced 48 TB of local NVMe SSD storage per ClickHouse node with S3 object storage + 2 TB local NVMe cache per node. Cold queries (first access to a date partition) fetch data from S3 at 1 GB/s via S3 Express One Zone; subsequent queries read from local NVMe cache at 7 GB/s. For their workload (80% of queries hitting the last 7 days of data), 95% of I/O was cache-served. Storage cost dropped 10×; query latency for hot data increased by only 15% due to occasional S3 misses.

keyTakeaways: NAND flash's erase-before-write constraint creates write amplification; optimize workloads to minimize WA or use enterprise SSDs with high endurance
NVMe's 65k-queue parallelism maps to NAND's internal parallelism; optimal io_depth 32–128 for throughput, 1–4 for OLTP latency
O_DIRECT is required for production databases to avoid double-buffering and correctly manage their own buffer pools
EBS is durable but adds 200–400μs network latency; instance store is fast (100μs) but ephemeral—use replication for durability
SSD p99 latency is dominated by GC pauses (1–10ms on consumer drives); enterprise drives with dedicated GC maintain sub-1ms p99
Tiered storage (NVMe cache + S3 object store) provides cost-efficient scalability without sacrificing hot-path performance
whyItMatters: Storage performance characteristics—write amplification, GC pauses, NVMe queue depth, and cloud storage tier economics—directly determine database throughput, transaction latency, and infrastructure cost. Engineers who understand NVMe internals can correctly configure databases for SSD hardware, design storage architectures that exploit tiering for cost efficiency, and diagnose latency anomalies caused by GC or write amplification rather than application code. The transition from HDD-era to NVMe-first design is still ongoing, and many systems inherited from HDD-era thinking leave significant performance on the table.
reflectionQuestions: Your RocksDB production database is burning through NVMe SSDs every 6 months. Walk through the metrics you'd examine and the specific tuning changes you'd make to extend drive lifetime while maintaining acceptable throughput.

Design the storage architecture for a hot OLTP database (10k transactions/second, <5ms p99) that must survive AZ failure without data loss using AWS cloud infrastructure. Compare three options: EBS only, instance store + EBS replica, and EBS + S3 snapshot.
Explain why a database that uses mmap() for data files but O_DIRECT for WAL is a reasonable design. What does each choice optimize for?
